tables.description: Ransacked emergency rooms, triage corridors, and sealed pharmaceutical dispensaries.
Industrial locomotives, maintenance pits, and heavy spare hardware stores.
Classrooms, administration records, science laboratories, and cafeteria stores.
Reinforced blast bunkers, weapon racks, and standard-issue ration stores.
Dense residential apartments with scattered domestic supplies and personal keepsakes.
Apparatus bays, rescue gear lockers, and high-durability emergency tools.
Flooded rail platforms, electrical utility tunnels, and emergency passenger shelters.
Evidence lockers, officer duty desks, and small-arms armory cages.
Metal stamping facilities, CNC lathe shops, and structural scrap piles.
Sprawling retail stores, stripped shelves, and backroom inventory crates.
Step-down transformers, switchgear banks, and thick copper transmission cables.
Corrosive chemical tanks, distillation columns, and hazardous reagent drums.
High-bay pallet racking with mixed industrial hardware, dry goods, and crated materials.
Cultivated fields, grain silos, seed sheds, and livestock pens.
Log sorting yards, diesel sawmills, and forestry maintenance huts.
Secluded timber cabins with field dressing tools, ammunition tins, and preserved venison.
Ancient stone vaults, herbal drying racks, and hand-copied illuminated manuscripts.
Outpatient consultation rooms, basic medical supplies, and iodine tablets.
Telescope domes, precision sensor racks, and optical electronics.
Glasshouse beds, irrigation tubing, seed cultivars, and growth nutrient concentrates.
A livestock surgery three years abandoned: the drug cabinet stands cut open, the hoist still hangs over the table, and the disinfectant smell never quite left the drains.
Four dental practices, three of them stripped to the walls by someone methodical. The fourth keeps its chair, its drill, its instruments, and its locked cabinet of small relief.
A hospice that ran through the worst of it and stopped on a day the charts still record. Beds made, lockers closed, the drug trolley parked where the last nurse left it.
A structure that came down and stayed down. Floors pancaked into rebar cages, plank stacks under dust, and the slow work of pulling building material back out of the wreck.
The scale pit still holds its counterweights and the office still holds its ledgers: every load that crossed this deck was weighed, priced, and signed for, right up to the end.
Dead vehicles stacked in rows by a crane that no longer moves. Engines hoisted and numbered, batteries on the shelf, fluids drained into drums nobody ever came back to collect.
Ranked storage tanks with fog-gauge ladders and vapour pockets between the bunds. The drums are stencilled, dated, and mostly still full, which is exactly the problem.
The roof is open to the sky and the stage is intact, and a whisper from the boards still reaches the back row. Someone keeps meeting here, and the aisles hold what they left behind.
Queue lines painted fresh on the pavement because paint is cheaper than riot control. What the crowd drops, the gutters keep: ration tins, blankets, and the notices nobody wanted to read.

Sandbags, a boom barrier, and a guard shack repapered with schedules nobody reads any more. What the garrison left behind is what the garrison considered ordinary: rounds, rations, and the forms that went with them.

A driving-licence bureau that changed its forms and nothing else. The ticket machine still works, the counters still stand, and the strongroom cabinet still holds the paperwork of everyone who was processed.

Two kilometres of hard shoulder marked in Garrison yellow, in a pattern the Garrison trained its people to read and everyone else learned to fear. Crated rounds, propellant drums, and the patrol orders that explain the paint.
The lattice mast stands over the ridge line and the hut at its base is powered — not preserved, not maintained: powered, drawing current from a source that has outlasted three years of no visitors.
Wall-sized route maps still sit under intact glass, annotated in grease pencil with times and transfers that correspond to no public timetable any more. Out back, the fleet sheds what it carried.

The ground here is not solid and never was. Cracks breathe hot vapor across the platform, boiling mud bubbles under a crust that looks safe until it is not, and the pipes still hiss from somewhere deep.

Blast doors still powered, still closed, and someone inside still answers the intercom. What comes through the hatch is what a sealed community stocked: filters, cells, and the records of who did not make it to the door.
A container-and-chassis market behind an electrified fence, where factor stalls trade copper, cells, and chips for whatever a hauler carried in. The stock turns over because the market is alive.
Pumps, gates, and the pipes between them: some still running, some drowned to their motor housings, all of them holding the water where somebody wanted it or lost it.
The deep end is a mattress floor now, and the tiled walls hold the heat the way they always did. The treatment room still smells of chlorine, and the tablets still purify what the taps deliver.
Rows of hives under mesh lids, a honey house with the extraction gear still in it, and the smoke pot by the door. Whether anything is still living in the boxes is a question the smoker answers.
A convoy's fallback cache, hidden properly the first time: fuel cans wired shut, spare parts in greased paper, and ration tins stacked the way somebody's sergeant liked them.
The town's memory in bonded leather: deeds, minutes, surveys, and the wills of people who owned things once. The preservation alcohol is drinkable, which the archivists knew and wrote down.

The presses stand ready and the ink drums are still sealed. Whatever the district needed printed last — notices, curricula, requisitions — is still in the racks, and the solvent still strips what it touches.
Deep shelves of the record as it was ordered to be kept: maps amended by decree, broadcasts transcribed before transmission, and the rad tablets issued to staff who were never told why.
The continuity stores: sealed ration pallets, service radios on charge racks, and a decontamination locker stocked for a evacuation that was cancelled rather than survived.
The lowest floor, where the air tastes metallic and every surface carries a faint permanent static. The detection equipment was left running, and the charts on the wall were updated to the end.

A market that trades out of boats at the drowned waterfront: ration tins moving one way, salvage the other, and everything priced in whatever the buyer is holding. The stalls restock because the trade route holds.
The priory keeps its dispensary stocked and its kettle on: bandages rolled, water drawn, and a bed for whoever asks. The stock turns over because the care does not stop.
Shallow pans evaporating down to their white crust, drying racks over the flues, and the salt traded out by the block. The camp works the pans in shifts because the pans never stop working.
